What adapters remember

When you fine-tune a public model on a few private images — especially with a small LoRA adapter — how much of those images is quietly recorded in the weights? This is a plain-language tour of what we measured, what we found, and what's still open.

Stance We observe, we don't conclude. Every leakage number is a lower bound for the weakest attacker — it says "at least this much leaks," never "this is the limit."

The question, and why it matters

A foundational result (Haim et al., 2022) showed that a trained network's weights secretly encode its training images — and you can reconstruct them. Our thesis carries that into the world of modern fine-tuning: foundation models adapted with LoRA, the small "adapter" matrices that everyone trains and freely shares.

The worry is concrete. LoRA adapters are tiny, so people pass them around like config files. If an adapter leaks the private data it was fine-tuned on, that's a real privacy problem. Our job is to measure — honestly — how much leaks, which things leak, and under what conditions.

The ruler — how we measure leakage

Everything rests on one honest instrument. Its core question: when we swap one private image for a near-copy, how much does the weight change? A big, distinguishable change means more of that image is written into the weights.

  • Whitened sensitivity d² = 2·KL — calibrated to equal the best-possible detector's signal-to-noise, and validated unbiased with a three-way cross-fit.
  • Detection p-value — a permutation test answering "is this leakage real, or noise?"
  • Valley width d*(0.1) — how tightly the weights pin down one exact image.
  • Recoverable directions r_J, q_eff — how many independent directions of the private data the weights actually expose.

The honesty rule

Every number bounds the weakest attacker — prior-free, adapter-only, per-image. It is a floor on leakage, never the reconstruction limit. We repeat this because it's easy to over-read a leakage number as "the most anyone could get." It isn't.

What we found

Each experiment probes one part of the same object — the gate-weighted weight update — read through that one ruler.

Who leaks · strong at n=12, softens at scale

Which images leak — and you can predict it without the adapter

A private image's leakage is predicted by its base-model gradient norm g₀ — how much the public model already "cares" about it. Correlation ρ = +0.86 at small scale, and the privacy chain closes: the images that leak most are the ones the model actually memorizes (ρ = +0.88). Honest caveat: the predictor weakens at larger scale (ρ = +0.78, graded indeterminate), and one out-of-distribution counterexample is still unexplained.

Activation crux · the supervisor's #1 question · confirmed on MNIST

The shape of the activation function decides how much leaks

Kinked activations (ReLU, leaky-ReLU, SELU) leak the most — roughly 5× more than smooth ones (GELU, softplus, SiLU) on MNIST. Smoothness anti-correlates with leakage, and the effect strengthens as the model changes more. It survived the realistic attack, not just the idealized one. It's a two-cluster effect (kinked vs smooth), not a smooth monotonic law — so we quote the robust facts (the 5× gap, the negative sign), not one fragile number.

Full-FT vs LoRA · n=6 · target-dependent

Full fine-tuning isn't a sharper memory than LoRA

We compared the valley width — the per-image sharpness — of full fine-tuning against a rank-8 LoRA adapter. The honest answer is ≈ equal, target-dependent. Full fine-tuning imprints more total signal per image (a bigger removal footprint), but not a finer memory of each one. Careful statistics mattered here: an early "full is ~17% narrower" reading turned out to be a two-target artifact — across six targets the geometric-mean width ratio is 1.02 (median 0.86), an approximate wash.

Reconstruction · full-gradient works · adapter-only is next

We can actually get recognizable images back

From the full-gradient weight change (the strong-attacker, known-recipe upper bound), reconstructions are recognizable across datasets — MNIST, CIFAR, Flowers (Fashion partial) — and even face structure at ViT scale. The robust adapter-only version of the attack (the weaker, more realistic attacker) is the clear next-weeks milestone. We're careful to label this the ceiling, not the adapter-only result.

Also

Multi-class looks like it leaks more. Switching the base task from binary to 10-class fills up the observable directions and dissolves the collinearity "wall" that had protected the hardest binary case — suggestive and exciting; a full replication is planned. And a side result: memorizing private images barely dents MNIST accuracy but can be catastrophic for Fashion — a genuine memorization-vs-utility tradeoff, worst exactly where memorizing is hardest.

Newest result

The adapter atlas — a real second channel

The freshest work asks a different question: not "can we get the pixels back," but does an adapter betray what it was trained on? We built a small "zoo" of adapters, systematically varying the training content, and clustered them by their weights.

Three findings point the same way. The weight change clusters perfectly by content (and by nothing else). A clean theory prediction is confirmed — the random-seed "junk" lives in the raw factors and cancels out in the product. And the strict, cheat-proof test agrees: +0.989 content recovery above a recipe-only baseline.

Scoped honestly — and it got sharper under scrutiny

A first-pass "indeterminate" was a cross-fit fold bug, caught precisely because the honesty gate flagged a suspicious exact-zero. And what it recovers is ≥ content-level — which digits were in the private set — not the specific images. It fades to near-invisible for single-image swaps. So the adapter records the concept, not the instance: a graded channel from +0.989 (content) down to ~0 (one-image swap). True instance-level recovery is the honest open item.

Where it's going

Primary axis

Direct weight inversion

Treat fine-tuning as a function of the private images and recover them by matching the weight change directly — the leakage upper bound.

The bridge

Gradient bridge

LoRA adapters are compressed recordings of the training gradient; a decoder trained on public proxy data expands them back toward the full gradient, then inverts.

New

Adapter atlas

Read the private makeup — which content, how much — off a population of adapters. First results are a real ≥ content-level channel.

A plain-language review of privacy-leakage findings from LoRA fine-tuning, MNIST-scale, as of August 2026. Extends Haim et al. (2022) into parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

Every figure and number here observes, it does not conclude, and bounds only the weakest attacker — a lower bound on leakage, not the reconstruction limit. Small sample sizes are stated where they matter. The full record lives in STATUS.md and the notes; this page is the tour, not the archive.
